To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
serotonin (5 HT) is involved in the modulation of esophageal sensation in healthy volunteers (HVs).
serotonin (5 HT) has no clear effects in esophageal/Gastrointestinal (GI) sensations.

1) esophageal sensitivity to mechanical and thermal esophageal stimulation is not affected by 5 HT, 2) esophageal sensation to acid reflux is not affected by a 5 HT antagonist and 3) 5 HT is not a mediator of the esophageal response to gastric distension.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of 1) 5 HT in the control of the esophageal sensitivity to acid, heat and cold and 2) the role of the 5 HT1B receptor in the control of acid sensitivity.
the role of serotonin in esophageal hypersensitivity in GERD.
the role of the 5-HT system in esophageal sensation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the role of 1) serotonin and 2) 5HT3 receptor blockade in esophageal sensation is not clear in HV.
the role of 1.5 HT in the control of GI sensitivity is complex, and that further research is needed to elucidate the role of 2.5 HT in GI sensitivity.

the role of 4-HT in the control of GI sensations is complex and that it is dependent on the specific sensory modality, the stimulus intensity, the type and the location of the stimulus, and the presence or absence of coexisting GI symptoms.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the 5 HT1A receptor agonist 8-OH-DPAT (8-OH-di-propyl-aminotetraline) does not alter esophageal sensations to acid, water, balloon and electrical stimulation.
serotonin does not play a major role in esophageal sensation in HV.
the role of 4-HT3 receptors in esophageal sensation is not as important as previously thought.
The main takeaway from our work is that
5 HT does not seem to play a role in esophageal sensory perception in HV.
the role of 4-HT in esophageal sensation is not straightforward.
5 HT does not play a significant role in the control of sensitivity to mechanical, acid, and electrical esophageal stimulation in health.
